claims.text: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles have enhanced configurational entropy and atomic-scale chemical complexity.
Configurational entropy and chemical complexity create locally stabilized atomic environments in the nanoparticles.
These locally stabilized environments delay the onset of surface premelting.
These locally stabilized environments broaden the melting transition relative to chemically simpler nanoparticles.
Multi-element interactions hinder early atomic mobility at the nanoparticle surface.
Chemical complexity causes thermal energy to be distributed non-uniformly in the nanoparticles.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are solid, single-phase, and chemically homogeneous.
Rapid solidification or inert-gas condensation can typically produce the stated homogeneous HEA nanoparticles.
Fluctuations in local atomic arrangement and chemical environment create energy barriers to rearrangements involved in surface premelting.
Multiple coexisting bonding environments impede surface-atom diffusion as temperature increases.
Impeded surface diffusion suppresses formation of a liquid-like surface layer until a higher temperature is reached.
Heterogeneity in local bonding energies spreads melting over a broader temperature range.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will begin surface premelting at a higher temperature than size-matched single-metal or simpler bimetallic nanoparticles under identical heating conditions.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a wider melting-transition interval than the baseline nanoparticles.
Well-studied Ag, Au, and simpler bimetallic nanoparticles exhibit more abrupt or lower-temperature surface premelting than the proposed HEA particles.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to chemically homogeneous HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–20 nm in diameter.
Significant phase segregation may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Outside the specified size regime, surface-to-volume effects may dominate the melting response.
